The Bransys electronic logging device has three hardcoded or cleartext credential flaws — CVE-2026-86520 (7.5), CVE-2026-86689 (5.9) and CVE-2026-77960 (5.3) — fixed in Android 11.00.00 and iOS 1.1.54. CISA’s machine-readable files now confirm four more. Modicon M340 and its X80 Ethernet modules (-04) carry CVE-2025-6625, a crafted-FTP-command denial of service scored CVSS v3.1 7.5 and v4.0 8.7, fixed from M340 firmware SV3.70 (with BMXNOE0100 3.60, BMXNOE0110 6.80 and BMXNOR0200H SV1.7_IR27 for the modules); it republishes a Schneider advisory first issued in August 2025, so the CVE year is not a typo. NetBotz 5, PowerChute and Edgenius are likewise republications of vendor advisories originally dated 11 August and 25 June. NetBotz 5 (-05) has an OS command injection, CVE-2026-13336 (v3.1 6.4, v4.0 7.3), plus CVE-2026-13337, fixed in 5.6.0. ABB Ability Edgenius (-06) inherits the Linux kernel “Copy Fail” privilege escalation, CVE-2026-31431 (7.8), fixed in 3.2.4.1. PowerChute Serial Shutdown (-07) has CVE-2026-13348, weak limits on authentication attempts (v3.1 5.3, v4.0 6.9), with version 1.6 as Schneider’s remediation. The Hitachi Energy advisory (-03) was not in the mirror when this card was first written; per reporting on Hitachi Energy advisory 8DBD000229, it covers CVE-2024-4872 and CVE-2024-3980 (CVSS 9.9), CVE-2024-3982 (8.2), CVE-2024-7940 (8.3, a service exposed without authentication) and CVE-2024-7941 (4.3) in FACTS Control Platform 3.4.0 to 4.1.1 where the GWS component is installed — see that advisory for remediation. CISA also updated ICSA-26-211-07, the Mitsubishi CC-Link IE TSN advisory, on 17 September, adding eight affected products. No exploitation is reported for anything in the batch, and none of its CVEs are in KEV; CISA’s KEV additions in the period were three Linux kernel flaws on 18 September (federal deadline 21 September, passed) and a Zyxel GS1900 switch flaw on 21 September, covered separately. The 22 September batch is covered separately. The two worth an oil and gas look are Modicon M340, a controller family common in utilities and balance-of-plant duties, and Edgenius, an industrial edge platform — judge both against your own estate rather than the sector labels. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-260-01 through -07 plus update ICSA-26-211-07 (17 Sep 2026); detail for -01 and -04 to -07 confirmed from CISA’s CSAF files, -02 from the advisory page, and Hitachi -03 CVEs per ISSSource reporting on Hitachi Energy advisory 8DBD000229 - Advisories published 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] ABB Freelance DCS controllers can be stopped by one crafted, unauthenticated network message — the fixes are already in shipped update rollups
item.category: Critical Advisory — Process DCS controller denial of service
item.description: ABB published advisory 7PAA010706 on 18 September for CVE-2023-5778, a missing length check in its Freelance distributed control system. An attacker with network access to an affected controller can send a specially crafted message that makes it stop; no credentials are needed. ABB scores it CVSS v3.1 7.5 (availability impact only). Affected are Freelance DCP, AC 700F, AC 800F and AC 900F controllers on Freelance 2013 and earlier, 2013 SP1, 2016, 2016 SP1, 2019 and 2019 SP1. The fixes already exist in Freelance 2013 SP1 RU06, 2016 SP1 RU07, 2019 SP1 RU03 and later rollups, 2019 SP1 FP1, and Freelance 2024, which is not affected. For AC 700F and AC 900F on Freelance 2016 and later, turning on Download-Protection from the Display Unit blocks the attack. ABB says the flaw had not been publicly disclosed or exploited when it issued the advisory. The sector link is our assessment, not ABB’s: Freelance runs process control in gas processing, compression, tank farms and smaller process plants, and many of those sites stay on older releases that never took the later rollups. - ABB cybersecurity advisory 7PAA010706 (CSAF), CVE-2023-5778; oil and gas applicability is editorial assessment - Advisory published 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] The OT Cybersecurity Coalition presses CISA again for a binding directive on federal agencies’ own OT, now citing the French refrigeration attack — a proposal, not a CISA action
item.category: Policy — Industry proposal for a federal OT directive, renewed after the French attack; no CISA action
item.description: CyberScoop reported on 6 October that the OT Cybersecurity Coalition has published a paper urging CISA to issue a Binding Operational Directive focused solely on operational technology at federal civilian agencies. The coalition wants the directive to assign responsibility at each agency, including an accountable OT cybersecurity officer, set minimum practices drawn from existing federal guidance, align with CISA’s 2022 Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals, and consider whether NSA’s OT guidance should apply to civilian agencies. In its words, “it is time for an encompassing BOD solely focused on OT security.” Earlier directives touched OT without being built for it. CISA did not respond to CyberScoop and has announced no directive. The paper leans on GAO-26-108937, published on 30 September: of 22 civilian CFO Act agencies reviewed, 15 had established inventories of networked IoT and OT devices, 11 maintained them, 10 included all required information, and only 7 met all three OMB requirements. GAO’s one recommendation is that OMB issue updated guidance covering these devices and oversee implementation. A directive would bind federal agencies only; the coalition’s argument is that it would also signal to the private sector what the government expects. On 14 October the coalition returned to the subject after the French supermarket refrigeration attack: in a statement reported by Industrial Cyber, it said failures in cybersecurity fundamentals had led to a significant incident, repeated ANSSI’s advice on VPN-only remote access, default passwords and firmware, renewed its call for a binding OT directive, and warned that refrigeration controllers could become an attack vector in the United States too, while noting that no US incidents have been reported. For oil and gas operators the practical value today is GAO’s three tests, which work as a self-check on your own OT asset inventory. - OT Cybersecurity Coalition paper as reported by CyberScoop (6 Oct 2026); coalition statement of 14 Oct 2026 as reported by Industrial Cyber (16 Oct 2026); GAO-26-108937; no CISA directive found as of 16 Oct 2026 - GAO report published 30 Sep 2026; coalition proposal reported 6 Oct 2026; follow-up statement 14 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] GAO: industry panelists, energy among them, say overlapping federal cyber rules are hard to satisfy while fighting an incident — and the CIRCIA final rule is now under White House review
item.category: Policy — Federal incident reporting; GAO report, no new requirement
item.description: The Government Accountability Office published GAO-26-109197, “Cybersecurity Regulations: Industry Panelists Identify Duplication and Conflicts and Ways to Address Them”, on 28 September. It records a virtual panel held on 16 July with six industry representatives from the energy, financial services, and healthcare and public health sectors. Panelists said it could be difficult to meet every reporting requirement while also remediating a cyber threat, saw DHS and SEC rules as duplicating sector-specific ones, and half of them agreed that progress on harmonisation has been limited. Their suggestions were consistent timeframes, thresholds and definitions; a lead agency, such as CISA, to coordinate reporting; and more collaboration between government and industry. Cybersecurity Dive reports that energy participants named TSA pipeline reporting and NERC CIP among the overlapping regimes. The report makes no formal GAO recommendations. It adds to a count already in circulation: on 8 September the McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce, drawing on GAO work, tallied 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. The rule most likely to change the picture has not arrived. CISA has now sent its CIRCIA final rule to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, which logged it for review on 1 October; the text is not public, the statutory deadline passed a year ago, and HIPAA Journal reports publication is expected before year-end. Once in force, covered incidents are to be reported within 72 hours and ransom payments within 24, from dates the final rule sets. Oil and gas operators will recognise the problem: one event can trigger TSA pipeline security directive reporting to CISA, Coast Guard reporting for regulated terminals, SEC disclosure, state regulators, insurers and contractual notices. - GAO-26-109197, with coverage by Cybersecurity Dive and Industrial Cyber; McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis as reported by Industrial Cyber; CIRCIA status from the reginfo.gov regulatory review record and HIPAA Journal - McCrary analysis 8 Sep 2026; GAO report published 28 Sep 2026; CIRCIA final rule received for OIRA review 1 Oct 2026, not yet published

item.title: [Info] CISA’s “Securing the Next 250” campaign: reduce attack surfaces, replace end-of-support devices, recover quickly — voluntary, but the end-of-support message lands on the field edge
item.category: Policy — CISA awareness campaign; voluntary, no new requirement
item.description: CISA has launched “Securing the Next 250” for Cybersecurity Awareness Month, as reported by Industrial Cyber on 2 October. It is built around three Rs: Reduce attack surfaces, Replace end-of-support devices, and Recover quickly to sustain operations. Acting Director Nick Andersen framed it around dependency: when critical infrastructure is disrupted, “so are the businesses and communities that depend on vital services.” Beyond the three Rs the campaign promotes logging, backing up and encrypting data, reporting incidents to CISA, and keeping an incident response plan that is exercised, with realistic drills that include leadership and legal counsel at least once a year, and it singles out replacing end-of-support edge devices. It is guidance and promotion, not a requirement. The fit for oil and gas is editorial but direct: this edition’s exploited edge flaws — MikroTik routers, Citrix and Ivanti gateways, Cisco SD-WAN and FortiMail — are the class of device the Replace message is aimed at, and remote sites are where routers, gateways and switches tend to outlive their vendor support. - CISA campaign as reported by Industrial Cyber; oil and gas framing is editorial - Reported 2 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] Texas Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian cites the tanker boardings and urges operators to “invest, test, monitor and strengthen” cyber defences — a statement, not a new rule
item.category: Policy — State oil and gas regulator statement; no incident reported; no new requirement
item.description: On 24 September the Railroad Commission of Texas issued a press release quoting Commissioner Wayne Christian, urging the state’s energy industry to prepare for evolving cyber threats. It is a commissioner’s statement, not a formal advisory or notice to operators, and it sets no new requirement and gives no technical guidance. It cites the August Coast Guard and FBI boarding of two foreign-flagged energy vessels bound for US ports, naming VL Prosperity, the crude tanker bound for Galveston (see the top story), and separate federal warnings that China-linked and Iran-affiliated cyber actors are targeting US critical infrastructure, including internet-connected operational technology and industrial control systems. It says it follows a notice the Commission sent to regulated operators earlier this year. Christian is quoted: “Texas is the energy capital of the world, and that makes our energy infrastructure a prime target for foreign adversaries,” and “We must invest, test, monitor and strengthen our defenses now.” He also calls for using AI to defend critical infrastructure. The statement reports no incident at any Texas operator and does not mention the Vivit Africa LNG carrier. For Texas producers, pipelines, processors and terminals, the practical read is that the state’s oil and gas regulator is publicly linking the maritime cargo compromises to operator readiness. - Railroad Commission of Texas press release quoting Commissioner Wayne Christian, as distributed via EIN Presswire and reported by World Oil; no incident reported - Issued 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA and FBI put a number on integrator risk: one compromised automation vendor, nine archives, roughly 800 files of customers’ SCADA information and schematics
item.category: Guidance — CISA and FBI joint fact sheet on third-party ICS integrator risk; no CVE
item.description: CISA and the FBI released a joint fact sheet, dated 23 September and publicised on 24 September, “Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working With Third-Party ICS Integrators”. It is built on a case from March and April 2025, when foreign cyber actors compromised the network of a US industrial automation company that provided system integration, engineering consulting and SCADA programming to industrial customers, including power utilities and transportation entities. Once inside, the actors searched for terms including “customers” and “SCADA” and staged roughly 800 files — customer SCADA information, ICS device details and schematics — in nine compressed archives for exfiltration. The fact sheet does not name the integrator, its customers or the actor, and describes no disruption. Its core advice is to limit every integrator connection to what a task requires and to replace continuous vendor connections with on-demand remote access that the operator enables, monitors and disables. No oil and gas customer is named; the relevance here is editorial assessment, because pipeline SCADA, compressor-station, wellsite-automation and terminal projects are routinely built and maintained by the same kind of integrator. - CISA and FBI joint fact sheet (dated 23 Sep 2026, publicised 24 Sep 2026), case details as re-posted TLP:CLEAR by WaterISAC and reviewed directly; also reported by Industrial Cyber and SecurityWeek; oil and gas applicability is editorial assessment - Dated 23 Sep 2026; publicised 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] NIST opens comments on SP 800-82 Rev. 4, the OT security guide most programmes cite — rebuilt around CSF 2.0 and zero trust, with comments due 30 November
item.category: Guidance — NIST OT security guide, draft revision open for comment
item.description: NIST released the initial public draft of SP 800-82 Revision 4, “Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security”, on 21 September, with comments due by 30 November 2026. NIST lists four main changes. The sector introduction expands to cover building automation, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels, and IIoT and cloud convergence. The guide is restructured around the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, and the old risk-management section is reorganised under the CSF Govern function. Guidance on implementing OT controls expands, including asset management and network monitoring and detection. The security architecture guidance now focuses on protecting system management functions and applying zero trust principles. Many oil and gas security programmes, internal standards and pipeline security reviews map to 800-82, so a revision changes the reference those documents point to. It is a draft, and nothing in it is binding until final. The comment period is the chance to say what does not work in a refinery or on a pipeline. - NIST CSRC publication page for SP 800-82 Rev. 4 initial public draft, reviewed directly; also reported by Industrial Cyber (22 Sep 2026); oil and gas application is editorial assessment - Draft released 21 Sep 2026; comments due 30 Nov 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s cyber decoys guide: tripwires and honeytokens as detection you can add without touching production
item.category: Guidance — Detection engineering for critical infrastructure
item.description: CISA published “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. The guide defines decoys as assets that appear to be legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract adversaries, detect their presence or support intelligence collection, and it structures deployment in three phases: preparation, execution and analysis. CISA positions decoys alongside Zero Trust rather than as a replacement for either segmentation or monitoring. The reason it is worth an oil and gas reader’s time is the constraint it fits: most detection improvements in OT require touching a production system, and decoys mostly do not. A fake engineering workstation credential that no legitimate process uses, a planted project file, a dormant account named to look like a vendor login — each of these produces a signal with a very low false-positive rate and no change to the control system itself. That makes it one of the few detection moves that can be made between turnarounds rather than during one. - CISA guidance “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response”, reported by SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber; OT applicability is editorial assessment - Guidance published 17 Sep 2026
